Question 1: Build an explain-to-me skill

Create a small skill named explain-to-me that helps you understand a homework question.

  1. Design your SKILL.md file so that, when you explicitly ask your agent to use the skill to read a homework question, the agent communicates with you and explains what the question is asking.

  2. Keep the skill file short. It should contain a few useful rules, instructions, and a clear statement of your intent. For example, you may ask the agent to explain the goal of the question, clarify what work is required, and point you to an appropriate section of the Week 3 lectures: Ridge Regression: Stability Through Shrinkage or From a Penalized Objective to a Fitted Ridge Model. The skill should help you understand the question without completing the solution for you.

  3. Create the skill yourself or with the help of AI. Save it as explain-to-me/SKILL.md. Then ask your AI agent to install the skill using its normal skill-installation method. Test it by explicitly asking the agent to use explain-to-me to read and explain Question 2.

  4. If the skill does not work well, or if it begins to disturb your usual workflow, ask your agent to remove the installed skill. You may revise and reinstall it if you wish.

  5. In all cases, append the complete contents of your developed explain-to-me/SKILL.md file at the end of your Homework 3 submission under the heading explain-to-me skill.

The complete file appears at the end of this submission under explain-to-me skill

Question 2: Ridge regression with nearly collinear predictors

Let n=100n=100. Generate mutually independent standard normal random variables

Li,Ui1,Ui2,Xi3,Xi4,i=1,…,n, L_i, U_{i1}, U_{i2}, X_{i3}, X_{i4}, \qquad i=1,\ldots,n,

and define

Xi1=Li+0.04Ui1,Xi2=Li+0.04Ui2. X_{i1}=L_i+0.04U_{i1}, \qquad X_{i2}=L_i+0.04U_{i2}.

Center and standardize each column of 𝑿\mathbf X to have mean zero and average squared value one, following the lecture’s scaling convention.

Continue to use 𝑿∈ℝn×p\mathbf X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p} for the standardized matrix and keep it fixed throughout the question, where p=4p=4 is the number of predictors. The unpenalized intercept gives p+1=5p+1=5 total fitted coefficients. Let

𝜷=(1.5,1.5,1,0)𝖳,𝝁=𝑿𝜷. \boldsymbol\beta = (1.5,1.5,1,0)^{\mathsf T}, \qquad \boldsymbol\mu = \mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta.

Generate a training response and an independent test response at the same predictor values:

𝒚=𝝁+𝝐,𝒚*=𝝁+𝝐*, \begin{aligned} \mathbf y &= \boldsymbol\mu+\boldsymbol\epsilon,\\ \mathbf y^* &= \boldsymbol\mu+\boldsymbol\epsilon^*, \end{aligned}

where

𝝐,𝝐*∼ind𝒩n(𝟎,𝑰n). \boldsymbol\epsilon, \boldsymbol\epsilon^* \overset{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim} \mathcal N_n(\mathbf0,\mathbf I_n).

Center the training response as 𝒚̃=𝒚−y‾𝟏n\widetilde{\mathbf y}=\mathbf y-\bar y\mathbf1_n. For each λ∈{0,0.02,0.2}\lambda\in\{0,0.02,0.2\}, fit the slopes using the lecture’s ridge formula:

𝜷̂λ=(𝑿𝖳𝑿+nλ𝑰p)−1𝑿𝖳𝒚̃. \widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda = \left(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X+n\lambda\mathbf I_p\right)^{-1} \mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\widetilde{\mathbf y}.

The unpenalized intercept is β̂0=y‾\widehat\beta_0=\bar y; add this training mean back when predicting either response. The case λ=0\lambda=0 is ordinary least squares. Use seed 43231 before generating the design and responses. R and Python use different random-number generators, so their exact numerical results need not agree.

  1. Generate 𝑿\mathbf X once. Report the correlation between its first two columns and its largest and smallest singular values. Use these quantities to explain why the estimator contrast β̂1−β̂2\widehat\beta_1-\widehat\beta_2 should be much more variable than β̂1+β̂2\widehat\beta_1+\widehat\beta_2.
Show the workflow 
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(43231)
n, p, repetitions = 100, 4, 200

# Generate the design once and keep it fixed for the whole question.
L = rng.normal(size=n)
U1 = rng.normal(size=n)
U2 = rng.normal(size=n)
X = np.column_stack(
    (L + 0.04 * U1, L + 0.04 * U2, rng.normal(size=n), rng.normal(size=n))
)

# Lecture scaling: mean zero, average squared value one.
X = X - X.mean(axis=0)
X = X / np.sqrt(np.mean(X**2, axis=0))

beta = np.array([1.5, 1.5, 1.0, 0.0])
mu = X @ beta
lambda_grid = np.array([0.0, 0.02, 0.2])

singular_values = np.linalg.svd(X, compute_uv=False)
print(
    pd.Series(
        {
            "correlation": np.corrcoef(X[:, 0], X[:, 1])[0, 1],
            "largest_singular_value": singular_values.max(),
            "smallest_singular_value": singular_values.min(),
            "condition_number": singular_values.max() / singular_values.min(),
        }
    ).round(4)
)

# Exact OLS standard deviations of the two contrasts when sigma = 1,
# alongside how far each direction moves the fitted values.
gram_inverse = np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)
a_sum = np.array([1.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0])
a_difference = np.array([1.0, -1.0, 0.0, 0.0])

for label, a in [("sum", a_sum), ("difference", a_difference)]:
    sd = np.sqrt(a @ gram_inverse @ a)
    print(f"{label:>10}: sd = {sd:.4f}, ||X a|| = {np.linalg.norm(X @ a):.4f}")
correlation                 0.9983
largest_singular_value     14.1730
smallest_singular_value     0.4061
condition_number           34.9007
dtype: float64
       sum: sd = 0.1003, ||X a|| = 19.9917
difference: sd = 3.4824, ||X a|| = 0.5775

Answer. The correlation between the first two standardized columns is 0.99830.9983. The singular values of 𝑿\mathbf X are 14.17314.173, 10.64610.646, 9.2539.253, and 0.4060.406, so dmax=14.173d_{\max}=14.173 and dmin=0.406d_{\min}=0.406, giving a condition number of dmax/dmin≈34.9d_{\max}/d_{\min}\approx34.9.

Both columns are built from the same latent LiL_i plus noise of standard deviation 0.040.04, so they carry nearly the same information. That shows up geometrically: ‖𝑿(1,1,0,0)𝖳‖2=19.99\lVert\mathbf X(1,1,0,0)^{\mathsf T}\rVert_2=19.99, while ‖𝑿(1,−1,0,0)𝖳‖2=0.578\lVert\mathbf X(1,-1,0,0)^{\mathsf T}\rVert_2=0.578. Moving along the sum direction changes the fitted values a great deal; moving along the difference direction changes them almost not at all.

For OLS with Var⁡(𝝐)=σ2𝑰n\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol\epsilon)=\sigma^2\mathbf I_n, any linear contrast satisfies

Var⁡(𝒂𝖳𝜷̂)=σ2𝒂𝖳(𝑿𝖳𝑿)−1𝒂=σ2∑j=1p(𝒗j𝖳𝒂)2dj2. \operatorname{Var}\!\left(\mathbf a^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\right) = \sigma^2 \mathbf a^{\mathsf T} \left(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X\right)^{-1} \mathbf a = \sigma^2 \sum_{j=1}^p \frac{\left(\mathbf v_j^{\mathsf T}\mathbf a\right)^2}{d_j^2}.

The variance is governed by which singular directions the contrast loads on, and each direction enters with weight 1/dj21/d_j^2. Here (1,−1,0,0)𝖳(1,-1,0,0)^{\mathsf T} lies almost entirely along 𝒗4\mathbf v_4, with d4=0.406d_4=0.406, and (1,1,0,0)𝖳(1,1,0,0)^{\mathsf T} lies almost entirely along 𝒗1\mathbf v_1, with d1=14.173d_1=14.173. Substituting gives standard deviations of 3.4823.482 and 0.1000.100 when σ=1\sigma=1. Their ratio, 34.734.7, is essentially the condition number, since dividing by d42d_4^2 rather than d12d_1^2 inflates the variance by (d1/d4)2(d_1/d_4)^2.

The difference should therefore be roughly 3535 times more variable than the sum. The data pin down β1+β2\beta_1+\beta_2 tightly but say almost nothing about how that total splits between two nearly identical predictors.

  1. Independently repeat the generation of 𝒚\mathbf y and 𝒚*\mathbf y^*, followed by all three fits, 200 times while keeping 𝑿\mathbf X fixed. Draw the training and test noise inside each repetition, then reuse that realized pair for all three values of λ\lambda. For each value of λ\lambda, report the empirical mean and standard deviation of

β̂1,β̂2,β̂1+β̂2,β̂1−β̂2. \widehat\beta_1, \quad \widehat\beta_2, \quad \widehat\beta_1+\widehat\beta_2, \quad \widehat\beta_1-\widehat\beta_2.

Also report the average training MSE and the average test MSE calculated from the independent test response, where

MSE⁡test=1n∥𝒚*−β̂0𝟏n−𝑿𝜷̂∥22. \operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{test}} = \frac{1}{n} \left\lVert \mathbf y^* - \widehat\beta_0\mathbf1_n - \mathbf X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta} \right\rVert_2^2.

Show the workflow 
# Axes: repetitions, coefficients, penalties.
beta_hat = np.empty((repetitions, p, len(lambda_grid)))
train_mse = np.empty((repetitions, len(lambda_grid)))
test_mse = np.empty((repetitions, len(lambda_grid)))

for k in range(repetitions):
    # One training and one test response per repetition, reused for all penalties.
    y = mu + rng.normal(size=n)
    y_test = mu + rng.normal(size=n)
    y_centered = y - y.mean()

    for l, lam in enumerate(lambda_grid):
        beta_hat[k, :, l] = np.linalg.solve(
            X.T @ X + n * lam * np.eye(p),
            X.T @ y_centered,
        )
        y_hat = y.mean() + X @ beta_hat[k, :, l]
        train_mse[k, l] = np.mean((y - y_hat) ** 2)
        test_mse[k, l] = np.mean((y_test - y_hat) ** 2)

coefficient_rows = []
for l, lam in enumerate(lambda_grid):
    b1, b2 = beta_hat[:, 0, l], beta_hat[:, 1, l]
    coefficient_rows.append(
        {
            "lambda": lam,
            "beta1": f"{b1.mean():.3f} ({b1.std(ddof=1):.3f})",
            "beta2": f"{b2.mean():.3f} ({b2.std(ddof=1):.3f})",
            "sum": f"{(b1 + b2).mean():.3f} ({(b1 + b2).std(ddof=1):.3f})",
            "difference": f"{(b1 - b2).mean():.3f} ({(b1 - b2).std(ddof=1):.3f})",
        }
    )

error_summary = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "lambda": lambda_grid,
        "training_mse": train_mse.mean(axis=0),
        "test_mse": test_mse.mean(axis=0),
    }
)

print(pd.DataFrame(coefficient_rows).to_string(index=False))
print()
print(error_summary.round(3).to_string(index=False))

   0.02 1.465 (0.145) 1.497 (0.148) 2.961 (0.104) -0.032 (0.274)
   0.20 1.355 (0.049) 1.359 (0.050) 2.715 (0.095) -0.004 (0.029)

Answer. Empirical mean with standard deviation in parentheses, over 200 repetitions:

λ\lambda β̂1\widehat\beta_1 β̂2\widehat\beta_2 β̂1+β̂2\widehat\beta_1+\widehat\beta_2 β̂1−β̂2\widehat\beta_1-\widehat\beta_2
0.00 1.290 (1.795) 1.701 (1.798) 2.992 (0.105) -0.411 (3.592)
0.02 1.465 (0.145) 1.497 (0.148) 2.961 (0.104) -0.032 (0.274)
0.20 1.355 (0.049) 1.359 (0.050) 2.715 (0.095) -0.004 (0.029)

Average training and test MSE:

λ\lambda Training MSE Test MSE
0.00 0.949 1.038
0.02 0.960 1.029
0.20 1.064 1.125

The simulated OLS standard deviations, 0.1050.105 for the sum and 3.5923.592 for the difference, match the theoretical values of 0.1000.100 and 3.4823.482 predicted in part (a). Setting λ=0.02\lambda=0.02 cuts the standard deviation of the difference by a factor of 1313 while leaving the sum essentially unchanged at 0.1040.104. The larger penalty λ=0.2\lambda=0.2 removes almost all remaining variability but pulls the mean of the sum down to 2.7152.715, well below its true value of 33.

  1. Interpret the coefficient estimates and test MSE using bias and variance. Explain why ridge can substantially stabilize the individual coefficients without producing an equally large change in the fitted values.

Answer. OLS is unbiased, and the table shows it: the sum averages 2.9922.992 against a true value of 33, and the individual coefficients average near 1.51.5. What OLS lacks is stability. Its individual coefficients have standard deviations near 1.81.8, larger than the coefficients themselves, so a single realization can easily report β̂1=−0.5\widehat\beta_1=-0.5 and β̂2=3.5\widehat\beta_2=3.5. Almost all of that variance sits in the difference direction.

Ridge trades that variance for bias. At λ=0.02\lambda=0.02 the bias is still small, since the sum moves only from 2.9922.992 to 2.9612.961, while the standard deviation of each coefficient falls from about 1.81.8 to about 0.150.15. At λ=0.2\lambda=0.2 the variance is smaller again, but the sum has been pulled to 2.7152.715 and bias now dominates.

The test MSE follows the standard decomposition. Because 𝒚*\mathbf y^* is an independent draw at the same design,

𝔼[MSE⁡test]=σ2⏟1.000+1n∥𝔼[𝑿𝜷̂λ]−𝝁∥22+1n∑i=1nVar⁡(𝒙i𝖳𝜷̂λ). \mathbb E\left[\operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{test}}\right] = \underbrace{\sigma^2}_{1.000} + \frac{1}{n} \left\lVert \mathbb E\left[\mathbf X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda\right]-\boldsymbol\mu \right\rVert_2^2 + \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \operatorname{Var}\!\left(\mathbf x_i^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda\right).

Estimating the two middle terms across the 200 repetitions gives

λ\lambda Irreducible Squared bias Variance Total Observed test MSE
0.00 1.000 0.000 0.039 1.039 1.038
0.02 1.000 0.002 0.027 1.029 1.029
0.20 1.000 0.109 0.021 1.130 1.125

The mild penalty buys a variance reduction of 0.0120.012 for a bias cost of 0.0020.002 and wins. The strong penalty buys a further variance reduction of only 0.0060.006 for a bias cost of 0.1070.107 and loses. Training MSE rises monotonically with λ\lambda, which is why it cannot be used to choose the penalty.

Ridge stabilizes coefficients far more than fitted values because the two live on different scales in the weak direction. Ridge multiplies the jjth singular direction by dj2/(dj2+nλ)d_j^2/(d_j^2+n\lambda). With nλ=2n\lambda=2 at λ=0.02\lambda=0.02, those factors are

0.990,0.983,0.977,0.076. 0.990, \qquad 0.983, \qquad 0.977, \qquad 0.076 .

The three well-determined directions are left almost untouched, and the weak fourth direction is cut to 7.6%7.6\% of its least-squares value. That fourth direction is exactly where the unstable difference lives, so the coefficient contrast collapses from a standard deviation of 3.5923.592 to 0.2740.274.

The fitted values barely notice, because 𝑿\mathbf X maps that direction to a vector of length d4=0.406d_4=0.406 rather than d1=14.173d_1=14.173. A change of size δ\delta in β̂1−β̂2\widehat\beta_1-\widehat\beta_2 moves 𝑿𝜷̂\mathbf X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta} by only about 0.406δ/20.406\,\delta/\sqrt2. Large corrections in coefficient space are small corrections in prediction space. The same arithmetic drops the effective degrees of freedom from 55 to 4.034.03 at λ=0.02\lambda=0.02 while the average test MSE improves only from 1.0381.038 to 1.0291.029.

Question 3: What does ridge regression shrink?

Let 𝑿∈ℝn×p\mathbf X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p} be a centered predictor matrix, and let 𝒚̃∈ℝn\widetilde{\mathbf y}\in\mathbb R^n be the centered response. Use the supplied predictor scales for this algebraic question; the columns need not have unit variance. Here pp counts predictors, 𝜷∈ℝp\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^p contains their slopes, and p+1p+1 counts all fitted coefficients, including the separately fitted, unpenalized intercept. Ridge regression minimizes

Lλ(𝜷)=12n∥𝒚̃−𝑿𝜷∥22+λ2‖𝜷‖22. L_\lambda(\boldsymbol\beta) = \frac{1}{2n} \left\lVert \widetilde{\mathbf y}-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta \right\rVert_2^2 + \frac{\lambda}{2} \lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_2^2.

  1. Derive the ridge normal equation

(𝑿𝖳𝑿+nλ𝑰p)𝜷̂λ=𝑿𝖳𝒚̃. \left( \mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X +n\lambda\mathbf I_p \right) \widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda = \mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\widetilde{\mathbf y}.

Explain why it has a unique solution whenever λ>0\lambda>0, even if 𝑿\mathbf X is rank deficient or p>np>n.

Answer. Differentiating the objective with respect to 𝜷\boldsymbol\beta gives

∇Lλ(𝜷)=−1n𝑿𝖳(𝒚̃−𝑿𝜷)+λ𝜷. \nabla L_\lambda(\boldsymbol\beta) = -\frac{1}{n} \mathbf X^{\mathsf T} \left(\widetilde{\mathbf y}-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta\right) + \lambda\boldsymbol\beta .

Setting the gradient to zero at 𝜷̂λ\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda gives

1n𝑿𝖳𝑿𝜷̂λ+λ𝜷̂λ=1n𝑿𝖳𝒚̃, \frac{1}{n} \mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda + \lambda\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda = \frac{1}{n} \mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\widetilde{\mathbf y},

and multiplying through by nn yields the stated normal equation, hence

𝜷̂λ=(𝑿𝖳𝑿+nλ𝑰p)−1𝑿𝖳𝒚̃. \widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda = \left(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X+n\lambda\mathbf I_p\right)^{-1} \mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\widetilde{\mathbf y}.

The stationary point is the unique global minimum because the objective is strictly convex. For any nonzero 𝒂∈ℝp\mathbf a\in\mathbb R^p,

𝒂𝖳(𝑿𝖳𝑿+nλ𝑰p)𝒂=‖𝑿𝒂‖22+nλ‖𝒂‖22>0whenever λ>0. \mathbf a^{\mathsf T} \left(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X+n\lambda\mathbf I_p\right) \mathbf a = \lVert\mathbf X\mathbf a\rVert_2^2 + n\lambda\lVert\mathbf a\rVert_2^2 >0 \qquad\text{whenever }\lambda>0 .

The first term is nonnegative and the second is strictly positive, so the Hessian 1n(𝑿𝖳𝑿+nλ𝑰p)\frac1n\left(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X+n\lambda\mathbf I_p\right) is positive definite and therefore invertible.

This argument never used the rank of 𝑿\mathbf X. If 𝑿\mathbf X is rank deficient or p>np>n, then 𝑿𝖳𝑿\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X is singular and the OLS normal equation has infinitely many solutions, since any vector in the null space of 𝑿\mathbf X can be added without changing the fit. Every eigenvalue of 𝑿𝖳𝑿\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X is still nonnegative, so adding nλ𝑰pn\lambda\mathbf I_p raises them all to at least nλ>0n\lambda>0. The penalty supplies the curvature the data fail to provide, and among the infinitely many vectors that fit equally well it selects the one of smallest norm.

  1. Let

𝑿=𝑼r𝑫r𝑽r𝖳 \mathbf X = \mathbf U_r\mathbf D_r\mathbf V_r^{\mathsf T}

be a compact singular value decomposition, where r=rank⁡(𝑿)r=\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf X), 𝑼r∈ℝn×r\mathbf U_r\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}, 𝑫r∈ℝr×r\mathbf D_r\in\mathbb R^{r\times r}, and 𝑽r∈ℝp×r\mathbf V_r\in\mathbb R^{p\times r}. Show that ridge multiplies the fitted response component in the jjth left singular-vector direction, for j=1,…,rj=1,\ldots,r, by

ρj(λ)=dj2dj2+nλ. \rho_j(\lambda) = \frac{d_j^2}{d_j^2+n\lambda}.

Suppose n=100n=100, λ=0.01\lambda=0.01, and the nonzero singular values are

d1=10,d2=2,d3=0.2. d_1=10, \qquad d_2=2, \qquad d_3=0.2.

Calculate the three shrinkage factors and the total effective degrees of freedom, including the unpenalized intercept:

df⁡eff(λ)=1+∑j=13ρj(λ). \operatorname{df}_{\mathrm{eff}}(\lambda) = 1+\sum_{j=1}^3\rho_j(\lambda).

Answer. Write 𝑿=𝑼r𝑫r𝑽r𝖳\mathbf X=\mathbf U_r\mathbf D_r\mathbf V_r^{\mathsf T} with 𝑼r𝖳𝑼r=𝑽r𝖳𝑽r=𝑰r\mathbf U_r^{\mathsf T}\mathbf U_r=\mathbf V_r^{\mathsf T}\mathbf V_r=\mathbf I_r. Then

𝑿𝖳𝑿+nλ𝑰p=𝑽r(𝑫r2+nλ𝑰r)𝑽r𝖳+nλ(𝑰p−𝑽r𝑽r𝖳). \mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X+n\lambda\mathbf I_p = \mathbf V_r\left(\mathbf D_r^2+n\lambda\mathbf I_r\right)\mathbf V_r^{\mathsf T} + n\lambda\left(\mathbf I_p-\mathbf V_r\mathbf V_r^{\mathsf T}\right).

The two terms act on orthogonal subspaces, so the inverse is obtained by inverting each separately. Since 𝑿𝖳𝒚̃=𝑽r𝑫r𝑼r𝖳𝒚̃\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\widetilde{\mathbf y}=\mathbf V_r\mathbf D_r\mathbf U_r^{\mathsf T}\widetilde{\mathbf y} lies entirely in the column space of 𝑽r\mathbf V_r, the second term contributes nothing and

𝜷̂λ=𝑽r(𝑫r2+nλ𝑰r)−1𝑫r𝑼r𝖳𝒚̃. \widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda = \mathbf V_r \left(\mathbf D_r^2+n\lambda\mathbf I_r\right)^{-1} \mathbf D_r \mathbf U_r^{\mathsf T}\widetilde{\mathbf y}.

Any component of 𝜷\boldsymbol\beta orthogonal to the columns of 𝑽r\mathbf V_r lies in the null space of 𝑿\mathbf X; it would add to the penalty without changing the fit, so ridge sets it to zero. Multiplying by 𝑿\mathbf X gives the fitted response

𝑿𝜷̂λ=𝑼r𝑫r(𝑫r2+nλ𝑰r)−1𝑫r𝑼r𝖳𝒚̃=∑j=1rdj2dj2+nλ𝒖j𝒖j𝖳𝒚̃, \mathbf X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda = \mathbf U_r\mathbf D_r \left(\mathbf D_r^2+n\lambda\mathbf I_r\right)^{-1} \mathbf D_r \mathbf U_r^{\mathsf T}\widetilde{\mathbf y} = \sum_{j=1}^r \frac{d_j^2}{d_j^2+n\lambda} \, \mathbf u_j\mathbf u_j^{\mathsf T}\widetilde{\mathbf y},

where the middle step uses the fact that 𝑫r\mathbf D_r and (𝑫r2+nλ𝑰r)−1\left(\mathbf D_r^2+n\lambda\mathbf I_r\right)^{-1} are both diagonal. Since 𝒖j𝒖j𝖳𝒚̃\mathbf u_j\mathbf u_j^{\mathsf T}\widetilde{\mathbf y} is the component of 𝒚̃\widetilde{\mathbf y} along 𝒖j\mathbf u_j, ridge multiplies that component by

ρj(λ)=dj2dj2+nλ, \rho_j(\lambda)=\frac{d_j^2}{d_j^2+n\lambda},

as claimed. Setting λ=0\lambda=0 gives ρj=1\rho_j=1 and recovers the OLS projection onto the column space.

With n=100n=100 and λ=0.01\lambda=0.01 the penalty enters as nλ=1n\lambda=1, so

ρ1=102102+1=100101≈0.9901,ρ2=2222+1=45=0.8000,ρ3=0.220.22+1=0.041.04≈0.0385. \begin{aligned} \rho_1 &= \frac{10^2}{10^2+1} = \frac{100}{101} \approx0.9901,\\[2pt] \rho_2 &= \frac{2^2}{2^2+1} = \frac{4}{5} =0.8000,\\[2pt] \rho_3 &= \frac{0.2^2}{0.2^2+1} = \frac{0.04}{1.04} \approx0.0385 . \end{aligned}

Including the unpenalized intercept,

df⁡eff(0.01)=1+0.9901+0.8000+0.0385≈2.8286. \operatorname{df}_{\mathrm{eff}}(0.01) = 1+0.9901+0.8000+0.0385 \approx 2.8286 .

The unpenalized fit would use 1+3=41+3=4 degrees of freedom, so this penalty removes about 1.171.17 of them, and roughly 0.960.96 of that removal comes from the third direction alone.

  1. Which direction receives the strongest shrinkage? Explain why shrinking this direction can reduce prediction variance. Under what circumstance could the same shrinkage produce substantial prediction bias?

Answer. The third direction receives by far the strongest shrinkage. Its component is retained at only 3.85%3.85\%, against 80%80\% for the second and 99%99\% for the first. Shrinkage is strongest where djd_j is smallest, because ρj\rho_j increases in dj2d_j^2 while nλn\lambda is the same in every direction. The relevant comparison is dj2d_j^2 against nλn\lambda: here d32=0.04d_3^2=0.04 sits far below nλ=1n\lambda=1, while d12=100d_1^2=100 sits far above it.

Shrinking that direction reduces prediction variance because the variance contributed by direction jj is proportional to ρj2\rho_j^2. Under Var⁡(𝒚̃)=σ2𝑰n\operatorname{Var}(\widetilde{\mathbf y})=\sigma^2\mathbf I_n, the fitted coefficient along 𝒖j\mathbf u_j has variance σ2ρj(λ)2\sigma^2\rho_j(\lambda)^2, so the total variance of the fit is σ2∑jρj2\sigma^2\sum_j\rho_j^2. A small singular value means the design barely varies in that direction, so the least-squares estimate of its coefficient is built from a small amount of signal and a full share of noise. In the corresponding coefficient direction the OLS variance is σ2/d32=25σ2\sigma^2/d_3^2=25\sigma^2, against 0.01σ20.01\sigma^2 in the first direction. Multiplying by ρ32≈0.00148\rho_3^2\approx0.00148 cuts that contribution by a factor of about 675675. Discarding a direction the data cannot resolve costs little and removes a large amount of noise.

The same shrinkage produces substantial bias when the true mean response has a large component in that direction. The bias along 𝒖j\mathbf u_j is

(1−ρj(λ))𝒖j𝖳𝝁, \left(1-\rho_j(\lambda)\right)\mathbf u_j^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\mu ,

so 96.15%96.15\% of any true signal along 𝒖3\mathbf u_3 is removed. If the response genuinely depends on that weakly observed contrast, ridge will fail to recover it, and the shrinkage that helped in the noise-dominated case becomes a large systematic error. This is exactly what happened in Question 2 at λ=0.2\lambda=0.2, where the coefficient sum was pulled to 2.7152.715 against a true value of 33.

Whether the trade is worthwhile depends on the signal-to-noise ratio in that direction, (𝒖j𝖳𝝁)2\left(\mathbf u_j^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\mu\right)^2 against σ2\sigma^2. Shrinkage helps when that ratio is small and hurts when it is large. The quantity is unknown in practice, which is why λ\lambda must be tuned from data rather than assumed.

Question 4: Ridge regression and optimization

Let 𝑿∈ℝn×p\mathbf X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p} be a centered predictor matrix with p=2p=2. Its columns need not have unit variance in this question. The intercept is fitted separately and is not penalized. Suppose the two eigenvalues of

𝑨0=1n𝑿𝖳𝑿 \mathbf A_0 = \frac{1}{n}\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X

are 99 and 0.010.01. Ridge regression with λ=0.09\lambda=0.09 has curvature matrix

𝑨λ=1n𝑿𝖳𝑿+λ𝑰p. \mathbf A_\lambda = \frac{1}{n}\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X + \lambda\mathbf I_p.

  1. Calculate the condition numbers of 𝑨0\mathbf A_0 and 𝑨λ\mathbf A_\lambda. Explain what the change says about the geometry of the ridge objective.

Answer. Adding λ𝑰p\lambda\mathbf I_p leaves the eigenvectors unchanged and shifts every eigenvalue by λ\lambda, so the eigenvalues of 𝑨λ\mathbf A_\lambda are 9+0.09=9.099+0.09=9.09 and 0.01+0.09=0.100.01+0.09=0.10. The condition numbers are

κ(𝑨0)=90.01=900,κ(𝑨λ)=9.090.10=90.9. \kappa(\mathbf A_0) = \frac{9}{0.01} =900, \qquad \kappa(\mathbf A_\lambda) = \frac{9.09}{0.10} =90.9 .

The penalty improves the conditioning by a factor of about ten. Geometrically, the contours of a quadratic objective are ellipses whose axis lengths scale as 1/ai1/\sqrt{a_i} for eigenvalue aia_i. Under 𝑨0\mathbf A_0 the axis ratio is 900=30\sqrt{900}=30, so the level sets form a long narrow valley: the objective rises steeply across the valley and is nearly flat along it. Under 𝑨λ\mathbf A_\lambda that ratio falls to 90.9≈9.5\sqrt{90.9}\approx9.5.

The shift matters almost entirely in the flat direction. The small eigenvalue is multiplied by ten, from 0.010.01 to 0.100.10, while the large one barely moves, from 99 to 9.099.09. Ridge adds curvature where the data provide almost none, which is the same fact that makes the estimator stable, since a direction with little curvature is a direction in which the fit is poorly determined. The contours remain elongated, so the problem is not perfectly conditioned, but a gradient method now makes far better progress along the weak direction.

  1. Gradient descent uses

𝜷(k+1)=𝜷(k)−η∇Lλ(𝜷(k)). \boldsymbol\beta^{(k+1)} = \boldsymbol\beta^{(k)} - \eta\nabla L_\lambda\!\left(\boldsymbol\beta^{(k)}\right).

Let 𝜷̂λ\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda be the ridge minimizer and define the optimization error

𝒆(k)=𝜷(k)−𝜷̂λ. \mathbf e^{(k)} = \boldsymbol\beta^{(k)} - \widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda.

Show that the component of 𝒆(k)\mathbf e^{(k)} in an eigendirection with unpenalized eigenvalue aa is multiplied at each step by

1−η(a+λ). 1-\eta(a+\lambda).

Let M=9.09M=9.09, the largest eigenvalue of 𝑨λ\mathbf A_\lambda. Find the interval of step sizes that contracts every eigendirection. Then compare these two choices:

  • For η=1/M\eta=1/M, calculate the two contraction factors and explain which direction converges faster.
  • For η=2.1/M\eta=2.1/M, determine whether the method converges. Assume the initial error has a nonzero component in the eigendirection corresponding to MM.

Answer. The ridge objective is quadratic with Hessian 𝑨λ\mathbf A_\lambda, so its gradient is affine in 𝜷\boldsymbol\beta. Since ∇Lλ(𝜷̂λ)=𝟎\nabla L_\lambda(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda)=\mathbf 0,

∇Lλ(𝜷(k))=∇Lλ(𝜷(k))−∇Lλ(𝜷̂λ)=𝑨λ(𝜷(k)−𝜷̂λ)=𝑨λ𝒆(k). \nabla L_\lambda\!\left(\boldsymbol\beta^{(k)}\right) = \nabla L_\lambda\!\left(\boldsymbol\beta^{(k)}\right) - \nabla L_\lambda\!\left(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda\right) = \mathbf A_\lambda \left(\boldsymbol\beta^{(k)}-\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda\right) = \mathbf A_\lambda\mathbf e^{(k)} .

Subtracting 𝜷̂λ\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda from both sides of the update rule gives

𝒆(k+1)=𝜷(k)−η𝑨λ𝒆(k)−𝜷̂λ=(𝑰p−η𝑨λ)𝒆(k). \mathbf e^{(k+1)} = \boldsymbol\beta^{(k)} - \eta\mathbf A_\lambda\mathbf e^{(k)} - \widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda = \left(\mathbf I_p-\eta\mathbf A_\lambda\right)\mathbf e^{(k)} .

Let 𝒘\mathbf w be a unit eigenvector of 𝑨0\mathbf A_0 with eigenvalue aa. Then 𝑨λ𝒘=(a+λ)𝒘\mathbf A_\lambda\mathbf w=(a+\lambda)\mathbf w, so 𝒘\mathbf w is also an eigenvector of 𝑰p−η𝑨λ\mathbf I_p-\eta\mathbf A_\lambda, with eigenvalue 1−η(a+λ)1-\eta(a+\lambda). Expanding 𝒆(k)\mathbf e^{(k)} in this orthonormal eigenbasis, the component along 𝒘\mathbf w satisfies

𝒘𝖳𝒆(k+1)=(1−η(a+λ))𝒘𝖳𝒆(k). \mathbf w^{\mathsf T}\mathbf e^{(k+1)} = \left(1-\eta(a+\lambda)\right) \mathbf w^{\mathsf T}\mathbf e^{(k)} .

That component is multiplied by 1−η(a+λ)1-\eta(a+\lambda) at every step, independently of the other directions, and after kk steps it has been multiplied by (1−η(a+λ))k\left(1-\eta(a+\lambda)\right)^k.

Every direction contracts when |1−η(a+λ)|<1\left|1-\eta(a+\lambda)\right|<1 for both eigenvalues of 𝑨λ\mathbf A_\lambda. For a positive eigenvalue mm this is equivalent to 0<η<2/m0<\eta<2/m, and the binding constraint comes from the largest eigenvalue M=9.09M=9.09. The interval is

0<η<2M=29.09≈0.2200. 0<\eta<\frac{2}{M} = \frac{2}{9.09} \approx 0.2200 .

For η=1/M≈0.1100\eta=1/M\approx0.1100. The contraction factors are

1−9.099.09=0and1−0.109.09≈0.9890. 1-\frac{9.09}{9.09}=0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad 1-\frac{0.10}{9.09}\approx0.9890 .

The strong direction converges faster, and in fact exactly: its error is annihilated in a single step, because the step size is tuned precisely to that eigenvalue. The weak direction contracts by only 1.1%1.1\% per iteration, so cutting its error by a factor of 10001000 takes roughly log⁡(0.001)/log⁡(0.9890)≈625\log(0.001)/\log(0.9890)\approx625 iterations. Since the overall rate is set by the slowest direction, the error decays at rate 0.98900.9890 once the strong component is gone. This is the practical meaning of the condition number: the iteration count scales with κ(𝑨λ)\kappa(\mathbf A_\lambda), which is why part (a) matters.

For η=2.1/M≈0.2310\eta=2.1/M\approx0.2310. The factor in the strong direction is

1−2.1×9.099.09=1−2.1=−1.1. 1-\frac{2.1\times9.09}{9.09} = 1-2.1 = -1.1 .

Its magnitude is 1.1>11.1>1, so that error component alternates in sign and grows by 10%10\% each step, diverging as (−1.1)k(-1.1)^k. The question specifies a nonzero initial component in this eigendirection, and the components evolve independently, so nothing cancels that growth and the method does not converge. The weak direction still contracts, with factor 1−0.2310×0.10≈0.97691-0.2310\times0.10\approx0.9769, but that is irrelevant, since divergence in one direction is enough. The step size exceeds 2/M≈0.22002/M\approx0.2200, which is exactly the condition derived above.

  1. Increasing λ\lambda generally improves the condition number. Explain why choosing λ\lambda to make gradient descent converge as quickly as possible is not a valid statistical tuning rule.

Answer. The two roles of λ\lambda are separate. The penalty defines which estimator is being computed, and the step size and iteration count define how accurately that estimator is computed. Choosing λ\lambda for computational convenience confuses the target with the algorithm used to reach it.

Following the rule to its conclusion shows the problem. The condition number

κ(𝑨λ)=9+λ0.01+λ \kappa(\mathbf A_\lambda) = \frac{9+\lambda}{0.01+\lambda}

decreases monotonically in λ\lambda and tends to 11 as λ→∞\lambda\to\infty. Perfect conditioning, and therefore the fastest possible convergence, is reached in the limit where the penalty overwhelms the data and 𝜷̂λ→𝟎\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda\to\mathbf 0. The rule would select a model that predicts y‾\bar y for every observation. It converges almost immediately and predicts nothing, because the objective being optimized so efficiently is no longer one that fits the data.

Statistically, larger λ\lambda moves along a bias-variance trade-off that the condition number does not measure. It reduces variance and increases shrinkage bias, and the value minimizing prediction error depends on the noise level and on how much true signal lies in the weakly observed directions, neither of which appears in κ(𝑨λ)\kappa(\mathbf A_\lambda). Question 2 illustrates both sides: λ=0.02\lambda=0.02 improved the test MSE, and λ=0.2\lambda=0.2, better conditioned still, made it worse.

The correct division of labor is to choose λ\lambda using an estimate of prediction error, such as the cross-validation or GCV criteria in Question 5, then choose η\eta within (0,2/M)(0,2/M) to solve that fixed problem accurately. If conditioning at the selected λ\lambda makes gradient descent slow, the remedy is a better algorithm, such as a direct solve, conjugate gradients, or momentum, not a different estimator.

Question 5: Selecting the ridge penalty for real-estate prediction

The supplied data/realestate.csv contains 414 real-estate transactions from Sindian District, New Taipei City, Taiwan. The quantitative response price is the unit house price. The six predictors are the transaction date, house age, distance to the nearest mass rapid transit station, number of nearby convenience stores, latitude, and longitude. Treat all six predictors as quantitative in this question. The column row_id identifies an observation and must not be used as a predictor.

The file data/realestate-split-folds.csv assigns 332 observations to the training set and 82 observations to the final test set. It also gives ten fold labels for the training observations. Match the two files using row_id and do not use the test responses while selecting a model.

Use the penalty grid

Λ={0}∪{10−4+0.05l:l=0,…,120}. \Lambda = \{0\} \mathbin{\cup} \left\{ 10^{-4+0.05l}:l=0,\ldots,120 \right\}.

For every fit, center and standardize each predictor using only the observations available to that fit, with the variance divided by the number of fitting observations. Center the response and leave the intercept unpenalized.

  1. Perform ten-fold cross-validation over Λ\Lambda using the supplied training folds. Estimate the predictor means and scales separately within each set of nine training folds. For each λ\lambda, calculate the mean validation MSE and SE⁡(λ)\operatorname{SE}(\lambda), the sample standard deviation of the ten fold errors divided by 10\sqrt{10}. Use this SE for the conventional one-standard-error heuristic. Plot the mean validation MSE and identify λmin\lambda_{\min}. Choose λ1se\lambda_{\mathrm{1se}} as the largest candidate in Λ\Lambda, including OLS, satisfying

MSE¯(λ)≤MSE¯(λmin)+SE⁡(λmin). \overline{\operatorname{MSE}}(\lambda) \leq \overline{\operatorname{MSE}}(\lambda_{\min}) + \operatorname{SE}(\lambda_{\min}).

Show the workflow 
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

data_dir = Path("data") if (Path("data") / "realestate.csv").exists() else Path(".")
realestate = pd.read_csv(data_dir / "realestate.csv")
split_folds = pd.read_csv(data_dir / "realestate-split-folds.csv")

# Match on row_id and confirm nothing is dropped or duplicated.
assert realestate["row_id"].is_unique
assert split_folds["row_id"].is_unique
course_data = split_folds.merge(
    realestate, on="row_id", how="left", validate="one_to_one", sort=False
)
assert len(course_data) == len(realestate)

feature_names = ["date", "age", "distance", "stores", "latitude", "longitude"]
X_raw_all = course_data[feature_names].to_numpy(float)
y_all = course_data["price"].to_numpy(float)
is_train = course_data["split"].eq("train").to_numpy()
X_train_raw, X_test_raw = X_raw_all[is_train], X_raw_all[~is_train]
y_train, y_test = y_all[is_train], y_all[~is_train]
folds = course_data.loc[is_train, "cv_fold"].to_numpy(int)

lambda_grid = np.r_[0.0, 10 ** np.linspace(-4, 2, 121)]


def fit_ridge(X_raw, y, lam, X_raw_new=None):
    """Standardize with the fitting rows only, solve, return raw-scale predictions."""
    n, p = X_raw.shape
    x_bar = X_raw.mean(axis=0)
    X_centered = X_raw - x_bar
    s = np.sqrt(np.mean(X_centered**2, axis=0))
    X = X_centered / s

    y_bar = y.mean()
    beta_hat = np.linalg.solve(
        X.T @ X + n * lam * np.eye(p),
        X.T @ (y - y_bar),
    )

    # Back to the original predictor scale; both forms give identical predictions.
    beta_hat_raw = beta_hat / s
    raw_intercept = y_bar - x_bar @ beta_hat_raw

    singular_values = np.linalg.svd(X, compute_uv=False)
    df_eff = 1 + np.sum(singular_values**2 / (singular_values**2 + n * lam))

    return {
        "y_hat": raw_intercept + X_raw @ beta_hat_raw,
        "y_hat_new": (
            None if X_raw_new is None else raw_intercept + X_raw_new @ beta_hat_raw
        ),
        "df_eff": df_eff,
    }


print(f"training rows: {X_train_raw.shape[0]}, test rows: {X_test_raw.shape[0]}")
print(f"penalty grid size: {len(lambda_grid)}")
training rows: 332, test rows: 82
penalty grid size: 122
Show the workflow 
fold_levels = np.sort(np.unique(folds))
# Rows are folds, columns are penalties.
fold_mse = np.empty((len(fold_levels), len(lambda_grid)))

for k, fold in enumerate(fold_levels):
    validation = folds == fold
    X_fold_train_raw = X_train_raw[~validation]
    X_fold_validation_raw = X_train_raw[validation]
    y_fold_train = y_train[~validation]
    y_fold_validation = y_train[validation]

    # Means and scales come from the nine fitting folds only, computed once
    # and reused for every penalty.
    x_bar = X_fold_train_raw.mean(axis=0)
    X_centered = X_fold_train_raw - x_bar
    s = np.sqrt(np.mean(X_centered**2, axis=0))
    X = X_centered / s
    X_validation = (X_fold_validation_raw - x_bar) / s

    y_bar = y_fold_train.mean()
    n, p = X.shape
    gram = X.T @ X
    rhs = X.T @ (y_fold_train - y_bar)

    for l, lam in enumerate(lambda_grid):
        beta_hat = np.linalg.solve(gram + n * lam * np.eye(p), rhs)
        y_hat_validation = y_bar + X_validation @ beta_hat
        fold_mse[k, l] = np.mean((y_fold_validation - y_hat_validation) ** 2)

cv_mean = fold_mse.mean(axis=0)
cv_se = fold_mse.std(axis=0, ddof=1) / np.sqrt(fold_mse.shape[0])
min_index = int(np.argmin(cv_mean))
lambda_min = lambda_grid[min_index]
one_se_limit = cv_mean[min_index] + cv_se[min_index]
lambda_1se = lambda_grid[cv_mean <= one_se_limit].max()

ols_position = positive_log_lambda.min() - 0.5

plot_position[positive] = positive_log_lambda


def penalty_position(lam):
    return ols_position if lam == 0 else np.log10(lam)


fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 4.4))

Answer. Ten-fold cross-validation over the 122 candidates gives

λmin=0.019953withMSE¯(λmin)=82.978. \lambda_{\min}=0.019953 \qquad\text{with}\qquad \overline{\operatorname{MSE}}(\lambda_{\min})=82.978 .

The standard error there is SE⁡(λmin)=19.230\operatorname{SE}(\lambda_{\min})=19.230, so the threshold is 82.978+19.230=102.20882.978+19.230=102.208. The largest candidate in Λ\Lambda whose mean validation MSE stays at or below it is

λ1se=1.584893. \lambda_{\mathrm{1se}}=1.584893 .

Two features of the curve stand out. It is almost perfectly flat from OLS through λ≈10−1\lambda\approx10^{-1}, with the OLS value of 83.01283.012 sitting only 0.0340.034 above the minimum, so the data barely distinguish these penalties. The curve then climbs steeply past λ≈1\lambda\approx1 as shrinkage begins to bite.

The standard error is large relative to that flatness. At 19.23019.230 it is more than 500500 times the gap between OLS and λmin\lambda_{\min}, because the ten fold errors themselves vary a great deal across folds of roughly 33 observations. The band is therefore wide, and the rule selects a λ\lambda almost eighty times larger than λmin\lambda_{\min}. That is the heuristic working as designed, preferring the simplest model statistically indistinguishable from the best, but the size of the jump is worth noting: the ten fitting sets overlap heavily, so SE\operatorname{SE} is a selection heuristic rather than an independent-sample standard error.

  1. Use all n=332n=332 training observations to calculate the lecture’s GCV criterion for each λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambda:

GCV⁡(λ)=MSE⁡train(λ){1−df⁡eff(λ)/n}2. \operatorname{GCV}(\lambda) = \frac{ \operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{train}}(\lambda) }{ \left\{ 1-\operatorname{df}_{\mathrm{eff}}(\lambda)/n \right\}^2 }.

Here MSE⁡train\operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{train}} is the training MSE, and df⁡eff\operatorname{df}_{\mathrm{eff}} includes the unpenalized intercept, as in Question 3. Estimate means and scales once from all training observations and keep them fixed for this calculation. Plot the GCV curve and identify λGCV\lambda_{\mathrm{GCV}}.

Show the workflow 
# One fixed full-training standardization, reused across the whole grid.
x_bar = X_train_raw.mean(axis=0)
X_centered = X_train_raw - x_bar
s = np.sqrt(np.mean(X_centered**2, axis=0))
X = X_centered / s
y_bar = y_train.mean()
n, p = X.shape
gram = X.T @ X
rhs = X.T @ (y_train - y_bar)
singular_values = np.linalg.svd(X, compute_uv=False)

gcv = np.empty(len(lambda_grid))
df_eff_path = np.empty(len(lambda_grid))
for l, lam in enumerate(lambda_grid):
    beta_hat = np.linalg.solve(gram + n * lam * np.eye(p), rhs)
    y_hat = y_bar + X @ beta_hat
    df_eff_path[l] = 1 + np.sum(singular_values**2 / (singular_values**2 + n * lam))
    training_mse = np.mean((y_train - y_hat) ** 2)
    gcv[l] = training_mse / (1 - df_eff_path[l] / n) ** 2

lambda_gcv = lambda_grid[int(np.argmin(gcv))]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 4.4))
ax.plot(plot_position, gcv, color="#2F6FB3", linewidth=2, label="GCV")
ax.axvline(
    penalty_position(lambda_gcv),
    color="#C84A16",
    linestyle="--",
    linewidth=2,
    label="GCV minimum",
)
ax.set(xlabel=r"OLS or $\log_{10}(\lambda)$", ylabel="GCV")
ax.set_xticks(
    np.r_[ols_position, np.arange(-4, 3)],
    ["OLS", "-4", "-3", "-2", "-1", "0", "1", "2"],
)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(frameon=False)

training singular values: [29.628 18.848 17.942 14.23  13.534  7.166]

Answer. The GCV curve is minimized at

λGCV=0.028184,GCV⁡(λGCV)=83.502. \lambda_{\mathrm{GCV}}=0.028184, \qquad \operatorname{GCV}(\lambda_{\mathrm{GCV}})=83.502 .

This sits close to λmin=0.019953\lambda_{\min}=0.019953 from cross-validation, one grid step away, which is reassuring given that the two criteria use different information. GCV needs only one fit per λ\lambda on the full training set, where the cross-validation estimate required ten.

The mechanism is visible in the formula. Training MSE increases with λ\lambda, but the denominator (1−df⁡eff(λ)/n)2\left(1-\operatorname{df}_{\mathrm{eff}}(\lambda)/n\right)^2 also increases as the effective degrees of freedom fall from 77 toward 11. For small λ\lambda the denominator correction wins slightly, which is why the minimum sits at a positive penalty rather than at OLS, where GCV⁡=83.581\operatorname{GCV}=83.581. For large λ\lambda the rising training MSE dominates and the curve climbs sharply.

The GCV curve is much smoother than the cross-validation curve and carries no fold-to-fold variability, since it comes from a single fit. That smoothness is a presentational advantage, not evidence of greater reliability. GCV still estimates prediction error from training residuals corrected by df⁡eff\operatorname{df}_{\mathrm{eff}}, and it inherits any misspecification in the linear model.

The training singular values are 29.6329.63, 18.8518.85, 17.9417.94, 14.2314.23, 13.5313.53, and 7.177.17, a condition number of about 4.14.1. This design is well conditioned, with no direction resembling the near-collinear pair in Question 2, so no direction needs heavy shrinkage. That is consistent with both error-based criteria landing on mild penalties.

  1. Fix all three choices before examining the test responses. Refit OLS and ridge at λmin\lambda_{\min}, λ1se\lambda_{\mathrm{1se}}, and λGCV\lambda_{\mathrm{GCV}} using all training observations. Report each model’s training MSE, test MSE, and effective degrees of freedom. Interpret the differences and explain why the model with the smallest observed test MSE must not be selected after viewing this table.

After matching the two files by row_id, use this order:

for each validation fold:

summarize the ten fold errors and fix lambda_min and lambda_1se

selected = pd.DataFrame(

CV minimum 0.01995 6.77321   80.13543  65.99957

Answer. The final comparison is

Rule λ\lambda Effective df Training MSE Test MSE
OLS 0 7.000 80.094 66.322
CV minimum 0.019953 6.773 80.135 65.999
One SE 1.584893 3.033 100.374 81.200
GCV 0.028184 6.689 80.171 65.903

OLS has the smallest training MSE, as it must, since it minimizes exactly that quantity using the full p+1=7p+1=7 degrees of freedom. Training MSE rises monotonically with λ\lambda across the table, which is why it can never be used to select a penalty.

The CV-minimum and GCV fits apply mild shrinkage, giving up about 0.230.23 and 0.310.31 effective degrees of freedom. Their training MSEs are nearly identical to OLS, and both improve slightly on the test set, from 66.32266.322 to 65.99965.999 and 65.90365.903. The improvement is small because this design is well conditioned, as part (b) showed. With no near-collinear direction of the kind seen in Question 2, there is little excess variance available for ridge to remove.

The one-standard-error model is different in kind. It cuts the effective degrees of freedom from 77 to 3.0333.033, so more than half the model’s flexibility is gone. Training MSE rises by 25%25\% and test MSE by 22%22\%, to 81.20081.200. Both move in the same direction, which is the signature of bias rather than variance: the fit is now too constrained to capture structure genuinely present in the data. The rule was drawn to this penalty by the wide standard error in part (a), not by evidence that heavy shrinkage helps here.

Why the smallest observed test MSE must not be selected. GCV shows the lowest test MSE at 65.90365.903, but adopting GCV on that basis would invalidate the number. The three penalties were fixed using training data alone, and that is precisely what makes the test set a valid estimate of future performance. Choosing among the four rules by comparing test MSE turns the test set into a fourth selection stage. The minimum of four noisy estimates is biased downward as an estimate of the performance of the rule that produced it, so the reported 65.90365.903 would become optimistic by an unknown amount, with no held-out data left to correct it.

The size of the difference reinforces the point. GCV beats the CV minimum by 0.0960.096 on 82 test observations, far smaller than the fold-to-fold variability seen in part (a). A slightly different train-test split could easily reverse that ordering, so the ranking between the two carries essentially no information. What the table legitimately supports is the weaker and more useful conclusion that mild shrinkage chosen by either error-based criterion performs about as well as OLS on this data, and that the one-standard-error rule over-regularizes this particular problem. Had a decision been required, it should have been made before the test responses were read.

Two further cautions apply. GCV is not an independent check on cross-validation, since it estimates prediction error from the same training fit by correcting training residuals with df⁡eff\operatorname{df}_{\mathrm{eff}}. Its agreement with λmin\lambda_{\min} shows that two training-based criteria see the same curve, not that either has been externally validated. And ridge only controls coefficient variance within the specified linear model. It cannot repair nonlinearity, omitted variables, or other misspecification, and a test MSE near 6666 against a response variance of roughly 185185 leaves room for all three.

explain-to-me skill

The complete contents of explain-to-me/SKILL.md:

---
name: explain-to-me
description: Use when I explicitly ask for help understanding a STAT 432 homework question. Explains what the question is asking without solving any part of it.
---

# Intent

I want to understand what a homework question is asking before I attempt it.
Explain the question to me. The mathematical, computational, and written work
stays mine.

# Instructions

- Read the entire question before replying, including any setup that appears
  before the lettered parts. That setup usually carries the notation and
  conventions the parts depend on.
- State the goal of the question in one or two sentences of plain language.
- For each part, say what kind of thing I have to produce: a derivation, a
  number, a plot, a table, or a written interpretation.
- Keep the question's own notation. Do not rename or redefine symbols.
- Name the one concept I need in order to start, and point me to a specific
  section of the relevant Week 3 lecture:
  - Questions 2 and 3: [Ridge Regression: Stability Through Shrinkage](https://teazrq.github.io/stat432rpy/topics/ridge-regression/ridge-regression.html)
  - Questions 4 and 5: [From a Penalized Objective to a Fitted Ridge Model](https://teazrq.github.io/stat432rpy/topics/ridge-regression/optimization-and-cross-validation.html)

  If you cannot read the page, say so rather than inventing a section title.
- Suggest a first step, then stop and ask me which part is still unclear.
- Keep the whole reply under roughly 300 words.

# Never

- Do not carry out derivations, algebra, or numerical calculations.
- Do not write solution code, pseudocode, or the sequence of fitting steps.
- Do not state the final answer, even partially.
- Do not confirm or reject an answer I propose. Ask me how I got it instead.

Reference

The real-estate data come from I-Cheng Yeh’s Real Estate Valuation dataset in the UCI Machine Learning Repository. The distributed data retain the original observations and add only the course train-test and fold assignments.
